name: GW World Heavyweight Championship
notes: The fed's own newsdesk of 30 March 2003 separately calls Lance Daniels "the GW Heavyweight Champion" in the same week its own news post of 28 March calls Silent Wind the new World Champion. Both readings stand; no seventh belt is recorded anywhere in the fed's own front-page championship row, which lists six.
epitaph: The belt the fed built its own last spring around, and it changed hands three times in six weeks without a single one of those changes happening in a GW ring. Maverick Reno lost it because Salaok fired him, and the co-owner handed it to Silent Wind, who said publicly that he felt cheated of it. Silent Wind carried it out of Global Wrestling altogether on 20 April 2003 and defended it on Primetime Central's own New Era supercard against Christopher Camero, in a traditional square ring the commentary said its own wrestlers had stopped being used to; Camero beat him with a superplex DDT and was still carrying it a fortnight later, when Jason Dynasty asked him for a shot and was told he was not at that level. Salaok is billed a five-time holder of it and Ben J. Pailthorpe a two-time one; neither reign is anywhere in the surviving record.

name: GW International Championship
epitaph: Crowned in a tournament whose final the record never resolves: the fed's own Clash of the Titans card of 28 February 2003 stages the final as its main event under two silhouettes, and its own newsdesk reports a fortnight later that an International Champion was crowned there. Derek Frost is carrying it a month afterwards, tagging with Jay Robson as ColdBlood and booked to defend it against Roz Blayze on 7 April. By WrestleCade III it is Tragic Hero's, and he keeps it in a four-way elimination match that Quartz walks into to spear the last man standing so that Tragic Hero can put him in the Perfect Circle.

name: GW Platinum Championship
epitaph: A belt that spent the spring of 2003 being taken rather than won. Venom Alexander was carrying it on 31 March when the arena screen cut to Leviathan going through his locker room and walking out with it, which Venom watched from the ring in the middle of a tag match. Mark Kullypso has it by WrestleCade III five weeks later, with nothing held saying how, and loses it there to Jay Robson and The Next Element — after which four Nevermore men lock the new champion in the ropes with a stack of chairs and Derek Frost comes down the ramp with a skateboard.

name: GW PrimeStar Championship
notes: Vacant before the tournament: the front page's own championship row shows the PrimeStar belt paired with the site's own mysteryman silhouette rather than a champion's headshot. The fed's own front page hangs its six championships in a row as belt graphics that swap, on hover, for the current champion's own headshot; three of the six pairings are independently corroborated by the fed's own show text of the same week, which is what makes the mechanism readable at all.
epitaph: Won in one night, by one man, in the only tournament the fed's record holds end to end. Six men were bracketed for it at WrestleCade III on 2 May 2003; Deacon Holmes came through a triple threat and Leviathan through a triangle match, and Leviathan took the final by refusing to let go of an octopus hold until Holmes passed out inside it. Its own name had been in the fed's rumour mill a season earlier — a match for it between Johnny Dollar and the Enigma was supposed to have happened at the previous pay-per-view and does not appear on that card.

name: GW Cruiserweight Championship
epitaph: Jay Robson held it into the spring of 2003 and lost it to Sage Sabbot in a ladder match in the last week of March, which is the whole of what the record says about how it moved. Sabbot was still carrying it at WrestleCade III five weeks later, using it as a weapon on the man who had just taken the Platinum title off Kullypso, and the ring announcer introduced him for the International title match with it in his hands. Roz Blayze won the right to challenge him on the same night, in a four-way ladder match for a replica of the belt.

name: GW Tag Team Championship
notes: The fed's own front page hangs its six championships in a row as belt graphics that swap, on hover, for the current champion's own headshot; three of the six pairings are independently corroborated by the fed's own show text of the same week, which is what makes the mechanism readable at all.
epitaph: The United Kings — the English Gent and Pete Hardy, billed together out of the land of warm beer and bad weather — are the only team the record ever places with it. They were booked to defend it against the Tragic Kingdom at Clash of the Titans in February 2003, and the fed's own front page was still pairing the tag belts with their photograph in April. The night that page was captured they had wrestled Venom and Cobra in a non-title match, and lost it by disqualification with the English Gent bleeding through a bandage at ringside.

name: GW Television Championship
notes: THE CHAIN OF THIS BELT IS NOT BUILT. Global Wrestling's own show texts carry at least twelve further changes and defences of this championship between 2004 and 2006 — among them a champion stripped for not defending it weekly, the vacancy that filled, and six other holders — every one receipted line by line in the federation's own scripts and none of them yet minted. What this record holds is one recovered reign inside a longer history, not the belt's lineage.
epitaph: A weekly television championship the federation defended almost every show, and one night of it survives in this record: 21 August 2005 at Evolution, in Las Vegas, where the masked Emoticon rolled the champion Dawn McFarlane up and the referee — the federation's own word for him is stunned — handed the belt over. He was still carrying it when the record runs out. The rest of the belt's life is in Global's own scripts and not yet chained here.

name: Iron Fist Championship
epitaph: Global's Iron Fist Championship's first recorded champion is Pete Hardy. The fed's own record carries 2 reigns on it, across 2 different champions.
notes: One line in the whole record: the four-man gauntlet on the oldest write-up, the Evolution of 19 February 2003, whose winner is hailed the new Iron Fist Champion.

name: Rising Sun Championship
epitaph: Global's Rising Sun Championship was first won by Cady Coleman on 2 December 2007. Cady Coleman held it at the end of the surviving record.
notes: Global Underground's belt, created at its first champion's crowning at the Underground of 2 December 2007, the last Underground show in the record.

name: Unsanctioned King of the Death Match
epitaph: Global Wrestling's King of the Death Match, billed unsanctioned. One crowning is recorded, 2005's, won across four Devil's Night death matches.
